The first week after the layoff, I had no structure at all. I woke at ten, scrolled job sites in bed, ate lunch at four, and by evening felt heavy and useless. On Friday I noticed it: the days with nothing fixed were the days I felt worst.
So I built a frame on the back of an envelope. 7 am: a walk round the lake, no phone. 9 to 1: applications and one hour of study, at the dining table, dressed as if for work. Afternoons: free. And one call a day with a real person. Shalini, my college friend, volunteered for Mondays and Thursdays.
It isn't magic. Some days the four hours feel like forty. But on the walk I sometimes think of a better line for a cover letter, and after talking to Shalini I remember I'm more than my job title.
— Preeti

subtype: Approach: routine to protect mood and energy [Thinking]

Career counsellor's note, 22 April.
Hemant came in two weeks after being laid off from the design agency. He said his days had "no edges": sleeping late, applying in bursts at midnight, not seeing anyone. He had noticed himself that his mood was lowest on the days with no plan.
We did not start with jobs. He sketched a daily frame himself: a 7 am walk to the tea stall and back, applications and portfolio work from 9 to 1, lunch with his mother, and one call or meeting with a person each afternoon. He said, "If I leave it loose, I'll drift."
We agreed he would try it for two weeks and tell me honestly which parts didn't work. He also has our helpline number in case the low days get heavier. Next session: 6 May.
— Jomon

qa.a: 7 am, to the tea stall and back.

For five weeks after the layoff, Tushar left his parents' flat in Andheri at 8.30 every morning in a pressed shirt, laptop bag over his shoulder. He spent the mornings in a public library applying for jobs and the afternoons walking by the sea to kill time. At dinner, when his mother asked how office was, he said, "Busy."
He couldn't say the words "laid off". His father had told every relative about his big job.
The shame grew heavier each week. He stopped sleeping. He skipped his cousin Hemant's birthday because Hemant worked in the same industry and might ask questions.
It came out in the worst way. His mother met his old manager's wife at the vegetable market, who said how sorry she was about the layoffs. That evening his mother sat on his bed and cried. "Five weeks, beta. You went through this alone."

The main language, fine, I knew it. Databases, fine. But in thirty-eight of the fifty there was one thing I had never touched: deploying to the cloud. That was my gap, staring at me.
I planned six weeks. An online course, two hours every morning, and one small project I could actually deploy and show. I felt silly starting from the basics. But in week seven I had a link to put on my CV, and the next interview asked me about exactly that."

Tushar, a friend from the old team, came over with samosas and helped count. "SQL, you have. Python, you have. Pipelines, you've built. But look." He pointed. "Cloud deployment. Thirty-one out of fifty. You've never done it."

With only three months, a long certificate was out of the question. They planned six weeks instead: a free online course every morning at the library, where it was quiet, and one small project deployed by week five. Gurleen wrote the dates on the wall above the cousins' TV.

Two months after the layoff, Elif had done eleven interviews in Istanbul and received no offers for product-manager roles. Her savings were thinning. Then Abebe, an old colleague now at an education charity, called. "We need someone for three months to redesign our volunteer sign-up process. It's not product management exactly. But it's close."
Elif hesitated. It felt like a step sideways. But the pay covered her rent and food, and it was only twenty-five hours a week.
She took it. She kept Tuesdays and Fridays for interviews and applications. The charity work turned out to use everything she knew: talking to users, simple prototypes, measuring sign-ups. In her next interview she had a fresh story: "Last month I raised volunteer sign-ups by a third."
By the end of the contract she had two offers.

Asif, you know how many final rounds I lost this spring? Four. I'm Kiran, and after the fourth I was ready to blame luck, or the recruiters, or my accent. Instead I did something awkward. I emailed all four hiring managers and asked, politely, "Is there one thing I could improve?"
Two replied. Both said almost the same thing: when it came to system design, I was vague. I'd draw boxes and say "this scales", but I couldn't explain how, or what would break first.
That stung. I'd thought system design was my strength. But it was clear. So for three weeks, every Sunday, my friend Rohit gave me a design problem and kept asking "and then what?" until I had real answers. My answers got shorter and more concrete.
In the next final round, they asked me to design a booking system. I got the offer, Asif.

qa.a: Two replied.

qa.a: It stung Kiran, who had thought system design was a strength, but it also brought clarity.

When I was laid off last year, I made a rule: I would only accept a job at my old salary or more. It felt like self-respect.
In month two, a hospital software firm offered me a role at ten percent less. I said no. In month three, Devika's company offered me a good team and fifteen percent less. I said no. Devika didn't argue, but she asked, "At what point would you change the rule?" I didn't have an answer.
By month six my savings were almost gone. I was lying awake doing sums. When an offer came at twenty-five percent less, from a company with a long commute and a manager who interrupted me twice in the interview, I took it within an hour. I had no strength left to negotiate or wait.
The job I refused in month two would have been better in every way. I just couldn't see it while I was protecting a number.

Thank you for the long call last week. I wanted to write down what we decided, partly so I remember it.
The first hospital recommended a treatment for Appa that would last at least a year. Amma was ready to start immediately. I was scared to question it; it felt like doubting the doctor. She went through it for forty minutes. She agreed with the diagnosis and suggested one change in how the treatment would be timed.
Amma feels calmer now that two doctors see it the same way. We start next week.
Gopika

"Our savings are almost half gone. And Amma is taking so many things now that the doctor doesn't even know about them."
Manjula stared at the box. "What if one of them is the one that works?"
"Then let's ask Dr Pillai. Tomorrow. Together. And bring the box."

qa.q: How much did the tablets cost?
qa.a: Eighteen thousand, for one month.

qa.q: Why does Manjula keep buying remedies?
qa.a: Manjula feels desperate and helpless, needing to do something while the doctors say wait for the next scan.

qa.q: What does Jomon suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Taking the box to Dr Pillai tomorrow, together, so the doctor knows everything Amma is taking and can say what helps.

qa.q: How is Jomon affected by the purchases?
qa.a: Jomon is worried about savings being almost half gone and about Amma taking things the doctor doesn't know about.

grounding: It shows a young adult, pushed by relatives' suggestions, spending savings on unproven remedies until Jomon urges checking with the doctor.
